title: Probiotics and Functional Microorganisms in Animal Nutrition: Mechanisms, Species-Specific Evidence, and Future Directions
content: The heterogeneous restrictions on antibiotic growth promoters across regions have positioned probiotics and other microbial feed additives as central tools for maintaining intestinal health and productive performance in terrestrial livestock (ruminants, poultry, and swine). However, their efficacy is highly dependent on strain, dose, animal species, and rearing conditions. This narrative review synthesizes recent meta-analytic and experimental evidence on the use of lactic acid bacteria (LAB), Bacillus spp., yeasts, and multi-strain formulations in ruminants, poultry, and swine, based on a structured literature search of peer-reviewed studies published mainly between 2020 and 2025. We discuss strain-specific mechanisms, species-specific value propositions, and emerging trends such as paraprobiotics, postbiotics, fermented feeds, and multi-omics-driven strain selection. Quantified findings include improvements in average daily gain of 18–22% in weaned piglets, increased villus height (SMD = 0.92) in broilers, and a 6.98% increase in ruminal microbial protein in dairy cows. We conclude that viable-cell probiotics currently have the most consistent evidence base, while alternative "de-activated" or "process-based" approaches have legitimate but non-substitutive roles. Sustainability claims should be anchored in verifiable antibiotic-reduction and food-safety outcomes rather than in circular-economy narratives.
